target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it
bullet_feedback.problem: Ownership and execution are ambiguous: 'Rebuilt' does not say whether this was a solo intern project or a team rewrite, and 'preferred it' is a survey preference, not adoption. The middle of the bullet is five technology names ('React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation') that push the outcome to the very end.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A hiring manager's first question is 'did this replace the old tool, and what part was yours?'. As written I can't tell if it shipped to the developer population or stayed a prototype that people liked in a survey, and the bold 90% draws the eye to the softest kind of metric on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the rebuilt app replaced the legacy tool / is in use by those developers; clarify: solo vs. team scope of the rebuild
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with what changed for developers (visual editor instead of the legacy tool), keep at most React Flow + Electron as the explanatory tech (the rest is in Skills), and state ownership/rollout status if true; consider unbolding 90% so a performance number carries the visual anchor.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by replacing a Claude skill’s open-ended search with focused sub-skills that call Python tools for workflow search and validation, guided by CloudWatch and OpenSearch latency logs
bullet_feedback.problem: Strong method + result, but 'AI workflow generation' never says who triggers it or what a 'workflow' is for, and the tail 'guided by CloudWatch and OpenSearch latency logs' is tool-naming that adds length without explaining the design decision.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader outside Capital One can't tell if this is a developer-facing feature with real users or an internal experiment, so the 65% is hard to weigh. The trailing clause makes the bullet run to the edge of two lines.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: who uses the AI workflow generation (the same developers as the rebuilt tool?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Tie it to the tool above in a few words (e.g. 'the tool's AI workflow generator') and trim or shorten the CloudWatch/OpenSearch tail to 'profiled with latency logs' or cut it.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
bullet_feedback.problem: The opening clause 'Because ... had strict access limits' is the hardest phrase on the page to parse: it's unclear whether 'access limits' means rate limits, permissions, or query quotas. The bullet also stacks two mechanisms (category tree + Redis cache) in one sentence, so neither gets explained.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most interesting backend constraint on the resume, but a reader has to re-read it to see the problem being solved, and a non-engineer recruiter will not be able to restate it.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'strict access limits' means (rate limit, quota, permissions)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Start with the action ('Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree...') and move the constraint after it in plain words (e.g. 'because the 270K-row table was rate-limited'); consider whether Redis caching is needed here given Redis caching also appears under TerpLabs.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo’s public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
bullet_feedback.problem: Excellent ownership/handoff story, but 'space-topic research tool' doesn't tell me what the tool does for the policy team, so the bullet establishes who uses it without what it does for them.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the clearest 'real users, real handoff' evidence on the page; a vague product noun weakens the first bullet a reader sees under a recognizable client name.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool does in a few words (e.g. collects/ranks documents on space policy topics)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'space-topic research tool' with a 4-6 word description of its function; the rest of the bullet can stay as is.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: Good design decision, but '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit (per day? total corpus?), so the scale behind the 34% can't be judged, and 'end-to-end latency' has no absolute value.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer will immediately ask 'latency from what to what, at what volume?'; without that, 34% reads as a relative number of unknown importance.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 6,000+ is per day/week or total; clarify: absolute latency before/after if known
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the time unit to the document count if it exists; otherwise keep as is rather than inventing a baseline.

bullet_feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often
bullet_feedback.problem: 'picks the right grasp more often' is the only unquantified, unscoped outcome on the page; 'tuned prompts' is also the weakest engineering verb in an otherwise solid pipeline bullet.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Next to precise numbers elsewhere, 'more often' signals that there was no measurement, which makes the research role read as light involvement. 'aimed at ICLR' with no submission status also invites a credibility question.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: how grasp choice was evaluated (success rate on a set of scenes, or qualitative), if any measurement exists
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: If a measured before/after exists, use it; if not, end on the concrete artifact (the overlay pipeline the VLM uses) and cut 'more often'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products
bullet_feedback.problem: Ownership ambiguity: the bullet credits the studio's output (110+ members, 5 products), not the candidate's own contribution.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For an engineering screen, 'co-founded' + org size reads as leadership signal but doesn't tell me what you built or led; a HM will discount it unless your role in those 5 products is clear.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: the candidate's role in the studio (e.g. leads engineering, reviews code, ran the product process)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep it short, but add what you personally run or own in the studio if true; otherwise consider merging it into the role line so the two engineering bullets carry this entry.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio’s class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
bullet_feedback.problem: The bullet ends at intent ('to reduce database load and latency') with no observed result; the only number (20,000+ visits) measures the product's traffic, not the caching work. It is also the second Redis-caching bullet on the page.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A HM reads 20,000+ visits as context for scale, then finds no evidence that the cache changed anything, and the repeated Redis-cache pattern makes the two bullets blur together.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: any observed effect of the cache (hit rate, query count, page latency), if measured; clarify: whether the candidate built more of Tortuga than the caching layer
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: If Tortuga ownership is broader, lead with what you built in Tortuga and mention caching as the technique; if not, consider cutting this bullet and letting the RAG bullet carry TerpLabs.

page_feedback.problem: Bold is spent on 90% (survey preference) and 93% (tester satisfaction) at the same visual weight as 1.26M events/sec and 12.8x.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: In a skim, bold numbers are what get remembered; two of the seven bold anchors are the softest evidence on the page and dilute the systems/performance story the candidate wants to communicate.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Unbold the satisfaction/preference percentages and keep bold on the performance and correctness numbers (65%, 34%, 50.9M, 12.8x, 1.26M).

page_feedback.problem: The strongest systems evidence (the IEX order book: correctness against real exchange data, data-structure choice, throughput) sits at the bottom of the page under Projects, below a one-bullet AWS role and a TerpLabs entry.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The intended profile is 'systems-oriented engineer'; in a 7-second skim the reader sees brands and AI-tool work first and may not reach the one project that proves performance-sensitive engineering.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Accept as a deliberate experience-first ordering, or reduce lower-value bullets (TerpLabs co-founding/Tortuga) so Projects starts higher on the page.

page_feedback.problem: Several outcomes are 'who used it' gaps: Capital One tool ('preferred it' vs adopted), UMIACS ('more often'), Tortuga caching (intent only). The Amazon Leo handoff bullet is the only one that clearly says real people now depend on the work.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Interview decisions for interns hinge on 'did it ship and who uses it'; the page answers that well for Leo and the IEX project but leaves it implicit elsewhere.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Where true, add rollout/adoption status in a few words rather than more metrics; do not add numbers that don't exist.

page_feedback.problem: The single AWS bullet ends with a dangling clause, '..., balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it', where 'it' is far from its referent.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The top-billed brand's only bullet requires a re-read to see that 'it' is the bounds logic.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Move 'and backtesting it' next to the verb (e.g. 'Writing and backtesting Java logic that sets...').

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine and replayed 50.9M real IEX exchange messages through it without ever resyncing to the exchange’s book, agreeing with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices

Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
Sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay, keeping each price level’s orders in a std::list FIFO inside a std::map and a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels

Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades its ratings, and fine-tuning runs only when the grades shift past a threshold

Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app, in which GPT-4o mini writes suggestions from scraped recipes found by SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB, and internal testers rated 93% of meals satisfactory
Clean single-column layout with right-aligned dates and locations and standard section headings
